newsitem.title: GUAM: More than 200 dead in S. Korean jet crash in Guam.
newsitem.headline: More than 200 dead in S. Korean jet crash in Guam.

text.p: More than 200 people died when a South Korean jumbo jet crashed and burst into flames after hitting an oil pipeline on this U.S. Pacific island early on Wednesday, Guam Gov. Carl Gutierrez said.

The Korean Air Lines Boeing 747 flying mostly South Korean tourists and honeymooners from Seoul crashed in rugged jungle area just miles from the airport as it prepared to land in a tropical downpour.
U.S. Navy officials said 33 survivors had been rescued and there was little chance of finding any others.
But in Seoul, a South Korean Cabinet official said about 50 people had survived the crash.
Construction and Transportation Minister Lee Hwan-kyun told reporters that he expected the number of survivors to rise, but did not elaborate.

At a news conference Gutierrez described the crash scene as eerie. "I heard screams from every corner of the darkness," he said, adding that he rescued about five people including an 11-year-old Japanese girl but failed to save her mother.
"You couldn't just stand there and allow the screams to go on without doing what you had to do," he said.
He said the plane burst into flames after hitting an oil pipeline that runs through the rugged jungle area that islanders call the "boondocks" just outside of the capital.

Airline officials said Korean Air Lines Flight 801 was carrying 231 passengers and 23 crewmembers, including dozens of vacationers, several South Korean politicians, three infants and at least 13 Americans.
Guam and other Pacific islands are popular destinations for South Korean honeymooners.

Airline officials said Shin Ki-ha, a four-term lawmaker and former parliamentary leader of the main opposition National Congress for New Politics, his wife and about 20 party members were on the plane coming from Seoul to Guam.
The plane broke into several pieces and there were reports that some survivors were trapped in the smoking wreckage of the tail section.
The National Transportation Safety Board launched an immediate investigation into the crash, chairman Jim Hall said at a Seattle news conference.
He said investigators would be looking in particular at a vital piece of airport safety equipment that was not in service for the landing.
Hall said officials on Guam had confirmed that the airport's glide slope, a device used for instrument landing during poor visibility, had been out of service for some time.
Hall said that instrument landings could also be made without the glide slope and there was no immediate indication as to what caused the crash.
Air safety sources said visibility at the time was limited to about one mile (1.6 km) due to the heavy rain.
Eduardo Cruz, a doctor at Guam Memorial Hospital, said staff members could see the flaming wreckage from the hospital miles away.

"We didn't hear anything, but we walked out and looked up and there was a big fireball on the mountain," Cruz told KCAL TV in Los Angeles. He said the hospital was about six miles (10 km) from the crash site.
Cruz said the site of the crash was "very dense, rugged terrain" and that it had been raining "rather heavily" in the last 2-3 days.
Ginger Cruz, spokeswoman for Gutierrez, said some survivors had broken limbs and the most serious ones were immediately taken to hospitals by helicopter.
A massive rescue effort was launched by the U.S. Navy and local civil defence and emergency services using U.S. Sea Knight helicopters and bulldozers to cut through the jungle.
All area hospitals were put on alert.
An FAA spokeswoman said the plane had just been cleared for landing at 2:35 a.m. local time on Wednesday (12:35 p.m. EDT on Tuesday) (1635 GMT on Tuesday) when radar contact was lost.
An emergency field hospital was set up by U.S. Navy personnel as close to the wreckage as possible.

Gutierrez told London's Sky Television conditions for rescue workers were very difficult and muddy. "You slip at every step you take and the choppers can't land except maybe about 200 yards (metres) away."
The governor said bulldozers were being brought in to carve out a road so that more emergency vehicles could be brought in.
"The tail section (of the aircraft) is still intact. The engines are laying around it. The mid section is completely burned out. The front end broke off on the other side of the hill."

Guam, largest of the Mariana Islands in the Western Pacific, is an unincorporated territory of the United States with a population of about 144,000. A U.S. military base covers about one-third of the island, the westernmost U.S. territory, which is located 4,000 miles (6,437 km) west of Hawaii and 2,200 miles (3,540 km) south east of Seoul.
